projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with James LeRoy Brown was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Let me just start by saying good afternoon.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Today is May 28, 2010. My name is Isabel Granados, and I'm the interviewer. I am conducting an oral history interview at the Court Reporting Institute of Dallas, in Dallas, Texas, with James Brown.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Will you please state your name and address for the record.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: My name is James Brown, and I live at 323 Rolling Oaks Ridge in Cedar Hill, Texas 75104.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Let me ask you. Why did you join?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Since I was a child I wanted to be a pilot. When I was a little bitty kid, and one time an old Army Air Force bomber, a big one at the time, landed emergency out close to my house and I ran out there, I didn't have a bicycle so I just briskly ran out there. And I was very disappointed he wouldn't let me look inside it. But, I've always wanted to be a pilot every since I can first remember and that's why I join it because the Navy was the one that I thought that I wanted to join because it was the hardest to get in to. And beside that I'd seen some recruiting posters of this handsome naval aviator in his white uniform and his beautiful airplane and so I thought that's for me, and that's why I joined it. The war wasn't really that important to me.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: The plane and the outfit?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yeah. The outfit and the plane and all those handsome naval aviators got dates with those beautiful girls, and that's why I wanted to join.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: My first day?

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Days in service.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Oh yes, yes. They were kind of difficult for most people. I remember mostly that we got off the train to the base that we were assigned to go to and, March the 9th, we got there, and marched up to this place and it looked like a big fortress and we thought oh my, where are we. And it turned out to be a University and we were in a University first and trained there first. And it -- we were -- our job mostly as enlisted cadets were to clean the toilets, polish all the things that would polish, sweep the floors, we learned -- we learned that we had to do everything from the very first and so it served us well I think later, later life we learned we weren't to good to do that.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Tell me more about your boot camp training experience.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: That would be what the -- would be called boot camp. Actually it was pretty nice. We lived in the student quarters in bunk beds. They were, as I recall it, three high. And we had to keep it polished and clean and everything, and we had to go the same thing. We learned how to March, we learned how to take orders and we learned how to respect somebody in uniform because we were just about the lowest run you can get. But I think it was well to know that people have -- do other things, they clean toilets and so they know that there's more than just the elite side of it.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So you start from the bottom up?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yes, ma'am. Absolutely at the very bottom. Plus another thing, they had a term they used "called washing out." I'd enlisted in a very elite group of people, we were totally selected, very difficult to get in but we lucked it and made it. But we learned that if we didn't shape up that we would be busted right back and sent back to a boot camp again as a sailor rather then as a pilot.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And what did that feel. Like in the beginning were you upset because you had to start from the bottom?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Oh no. We were delighted, I was delighted that I was in that way because, as a -- in high school I was pretty much of a misfit, and an average student. To even get in to this outfit I had to be strive to do it, and in fact I'm quite sure if it hadn't of been the war time I'd never gotten in it. So I was delighted to do anything to keep in there.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And which war did you serve in?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I served in World War II. It had actually been going on not quite a year. In October of 1942 and then I served totally as a reserve after World War II was over I stayed in the reserve still flew fighter planes in the reserve on weekends. And then when the Korean war came back along I asked the Navy to put me back on active duty and flew in the Korean War as well, and then after that was over I came back on -- off of active duty and served in the organized reserve, as they call it, or the radio reserve. Still flying then I became a commanding officer of a squatter and I stayed in there until I got to old to fly and then after I was 40, when they made you quite flying super sonic airplanes. Then I was transferred into the staff and then after -- I think 3 years after that then I retired as a -- and a -- and retired and -- went to retirement I should say. But did not get paid until I got to the age of 60-years-old then I got my pension at that time.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: So I was really a civilian during those years, but I was also a half-way military at the time.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: In World War II I was trained in Texas, in Corpus Christi. But I was also trained in various basis in the United States. In Kansas, in California, and got my wings in Corpus Christi, Texas at the naval air station. And from there I was trained in what they called in operational training with the fighter planes, in Florida. And from there I was transferred from a fighter squadron that left for the combat and they picked me, along with a few other people in the Navy. And we went to a new organization, the Mayfair [SIC] Program and so I was still three more months in Florida and then from there I was sent to Hawaii for final training and from there I went back to the fleet. And that was in World War II. Then, from there I was on Saipan and then on aircraft carriers -- I was on the smaller aircraft carriers in World War II, what we called the jeep carriers, and they were very small carries. Some of them were converted to night fighter carriers and some of them were regular carriers and I did not see a lot of combat in World War II. I wanted to, but they transferred us to the Marine Core believe it or not, and they were training us for the invasion of Japan and I went on a few of the missions with the Marines against land islands, or targets on land, but not very much. And very frankly the only Japanese plane I ever saw in the air, a guy almost killed me. I mean these Japanese pilots were very well trained and they were darn good at flying great airplanes. And, but then -- the -- I only have strafed a few times. I've killed people. I understand I didn't like that, but I did catch a Japanese plane on the ground one time and strafed it and blew it apart, but nothing spectacular like a lot of the people I'm sure your going to interview.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: How did that feel?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I thoroughly enjoyed it, I really did. It's an interesting thing. Now you wont think about it, but at that time -- now remember we were (versly) teenagers. And I was out to win the war for the United States you know, and so boy if I could kill any Jap's I was all happy about that. It wasn't until the Korean War whether I knew I met some Japanese pilots that had fought against our forces in the pacific with me and they had the same thing that we did they had the same problems and at that time I was married and had two children and so did the guy I met. The difference between the two of us -- we were the same age even -- so we met and we talked and compared notes and I got permission from the naval intelligence to invite he and his wife aboard the aircraft carrier for dinner. That was during the time of Korea. And the difference between the two of us, we had a parallel career, almost exactly. He fought against us in the Word War II. And then he became a civilian and then when the Korean War came back and I was recalled back to active duty he had just gotten recalled to the Japanese Navy the cost of defense force, they called it to active duty again. And the difference between us was the fact that he had 26 American planes he had shot down and I hadn't shot down any. So that's a lot of difference. But we had very similar backgrounds, and so I learned then, that -- they weren't as bad of people as we had been told.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And you found that out when you met them.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: You found that out when you met them.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Right, when I met him personally.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Do you remember arriving first there -- did you first -- do you remember first arriving there, how it felt like?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Arriving where?

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Where you first went for war.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Oh yeah. Yes I do, because when we -- now this is going back to World War II now. Been sent to Hawaii for final training as, as a night fighter actually. Still flying a fighter plane, but a special version of the fighter planes. Had radar and we were trained to make an interception and this kind of thing. So then one day, or one evening rather. The commanding officers called, and called me into his office and he said your leaving in the morning. And so myself and three of my team -- teammates we were trained as a team. We were trained as a team and flew as a team. Two at one time and two at another time. Which is highly unusual because in those days they had these big large number of planes flying, but we were specialist. So we were taken the next morning and we were brand new, and very low ranking innocence you know, just one little bar. And thought we were the best thing in the world, Gods gift to the women and fighter planes you know. Anyway, they put us on a four engine transport plane, and we were the youngest and -- the people we were the most purposed people there. It was filled with admirals and four strip we were flown in high priority planes those days to even fly on one and they flew us across to qualm and from there the next morning they said a report to you -- to the base immediately and take all your gear and so we jumped in a jeep, got on this plane and then we flew out there and we were just ready to go to combat. So we were really looking forward to it. I don't know of anybody in my group that was ever afraid of anything, we were just looking forward to it, it was just something different.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Was it something you expected?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Oh yeah. We trained for it, and prayed for it really, we wanted to. There's no such thing in those days of anybody -- at least to my knowledge that was afraid, they were always looking forward to the adventure.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Okay. Tell me about a couple of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Well, in World War II one of the most memorable experience was this time when the Japanese plane -- the Japanese guy almost killed me. That was -- it was kind of interesting at that. We was on a -- we were on a night patrol and the terminology was called combat air patrol and so, at that time I was flying with the marines as a Navy pilot and so we would be taken and ordered out, four of us. To the four quadrants around a big island -- an island where we were based at the time. And so we would go up and we would fly and this one quadrant, and that was our assigned altitude -- our assigned area. And another one of my teammates would fly on the other quadrants of the four. And so then if an air plane, or what they call a bogie came in, which was an unidentified air plane. It could have been an American air plane, or could have been a Japanese. And so we were always under alert all the time. And so that time my engine was running a little bit rough and so my time was just about up and so I called in on the radio and told them -- reported in, and they ordered me back to base. And on the way back they called me and they were -- at that time they were going to send another to replace me. At that time when they called me I turned out to be the closest one to this unidentified plane. So they ordered me back to there, so that took priority of whether my engine was running rough or not. And I turned towards it and tried to intercept it and we were controlled by radar from the island itself, and so they vectered me to a certain -- to a certain heading, and luckily I did intercept this Japanese plane but it was at night so I couldn't see him, so I got closer and closer to him and he was doing about the same speed as me and I thought well it must be one of the American B-29s because they were actually faster then our fighter planes, which the public didn't know about at the time. And anyway I thought well he's probably coming back shot up and lost his heading or lost he has compass or something, because he was making different directions and I would turn towards him and he would turn away but he was about the same speed as me. But I didn't realize that he was getting lower and lower and so then we got into the rain and rain squall and it was the black of the night and it got closer and closer and so in those days we had a radio -- what they called a radio altimeter on our air plane. And so you would set it when you left, so if you accidently got to low over the water or something it would flash red and I always had mine set at a hundred feet. I'm using my hands now, but -- but I was trying to intercept this fellow but he was going as fast as me and maybe a little faster. But he was getting me lower and lower and lower and I didn't realize it because I was on _____+ watch my radar and flying and everything. And all of a sudden this light on my radio flashed red like this and got my attention and just as it happened that men I was a hundred feet over the water and probably lower and at a high rate of speed and then suddenly flame come past me and later I realized what it was that I had been on the tail of this four engine bomber what turned out to be a Japanese patrol bomber initially a slow air plane diving all of this time just as I got really down low like this he culled his four engines off and bombed them /TPHRAPL came out I'm sure he expected me to drive and because I was so shocked I didn't do anything it saved my life. I could remember to this day and some times wake up at night I can see those big red balls as and so I never could find him after that, but he was a -- you know this made me feel very, very embarrassed because he was a big old slow air plane and he made me look like a fool real professional. He knew what he was doing and I just -- was just a young kid, didn't know the difference to be very careful and I never did tell the Navy about that. I said I just lost contact and couldn't find him. That was one of them but there's a More air plane and um it was on in the same roughly the same time and this air plane on that air plane and on the island we had the hospital, had a hospital ship their for the more serious wounds that fly invasion of the island or when they would take them back from some other place they would fly them in seriously wounded people. Anyway, I was vectored in on another one one time very close to the island, and so I came in behind him and I -- and of course we had our guns charged and ready to fire were turned on and so he was doing this violent maneuvering like this and I was getting to the trying to to get to the position to fire and then on the radio they kept the guy was not talking and couldn't talk to us and so they presumed it was Japanese and all of the bombers we had were lined up ready to fly so we knew it would be a disaster and so they said fire at will fired I had him for some reason I noted I glanced up well that's not something he had his lights on because at night and so I realized that it was an American hospital plan and I'd been open at fire to will to shoot him down looked up and that would have been all those people the wounded people and they were lit litter cases that they call them and so that was one of the most memorable things that I -- I didn't have the horrible stories like a lot of the other people I'm sure your going to interview. But, but that was -- could've been a disaster certainly of friendly fire. But that's a couple of them, but nothing really bad in World War II. I wasn't hurt. I was a young officer. Very very impressed with myself. I'd put my shows out of the door in where we stayed in the little state rooms on the carrier and we had clean sheets after all you see I was a boy scout and I learned very quickly I didn't want to be a soldier cause they crawled around in the dirt and stuff with spiders and I thought the Navy eats well, and I found out that they did. It was very nice and I'd recommend anybody for the Navy. You still get shot at, but the bullets are cleaner.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So do you still have dreams or nightmares?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: You do?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yeah. There's some things I'd rather not tell you that are -- were not fun and I, um not of fare like some people I've heard of that would sum up and still wake up screaming but some of the things that we did experience that, you know don't want to talk about particularly. When we were on the honors flight up to Washington we got to go to the -- to the hospital up there I forget the name momentarily -- and we met some of the soldiers and ended to visits with us and so we talk today one and this one kid was, came around and he was highly agitated and jumping up and down and I came up and he was like this and just vibrating over there and I said when he came up I shock up and I said I know what your going through and we had a nice visit little bit most of us have had a little bit of stress you know some of us have never lot it yet, for example, now I'm 87 and I was in the war since I was 19 or something and I was in two wars and even to this day I don't have a gun. Don't want a gun, and I don't ever every kill /SPWEPBL anything and I'm terrified of spiders but I won't even kill a spider and so its just one of those things but it's just something that you get so sick of it I guess maybe that's what it was, that's all.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: That's good, I mean you don't want to have to say what you don't want to.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yeah, even to this day there's a few every now and then I'll have a dream you know. I guess you never loose all of that stuff but some of them don't want to know about, but I noticed one of the things at our honor flight when we went to Washington and this might be interesting hear for you, at the end of the time we were there we had a ban quit and at the end of the bang quit one of the -- you people that were kind of in charge of it asked if anybody like to say anything and after a while a couple of the fellows said yeah I'd like to say something tell personal stories kind of like we're talking about now. And -- I realized very quickly these were the stories they were talking just for us who had been in the service at that time. We're listening to things that happened to them that you could tell that they had never told their family, or their wives or anybody because they were so terribly horrible. And the more I listened to the fellows tell us some of those things -- like one was a survivor of the Patan death March. Another was a Jewish fellow that had been in the Army and had helped liberate one of those death camps that the Nazi's had, and he told some of the stories there of what happened as they got there. And the -- like the Germans had machine guns women and kids right before as they got there. And some of these horrible horrible things that I realized that is was a cathartic thing for them, and so that's some of the stuff that, that probably nobody wants to tell you here on one of these interviews.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Okay. With that being said. Let's talk briefly an your accomplishments.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Okay great! I was a hero, in my own mind.(laughter)

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yes, I was. I was -- I only got in one battle in World War II, and I didn't win any medals in World War II. But in the Korean War I was awarded the distinguished flyers cross, and three air medals, which was some what unique since it was all at night, I was still a night fighter in the Korean War. And so those were the only declaration that I got I have 17 medals and area ribbons and stuff like that, but I thought they were kind of pretty, anyway and there was I got recommended for one that I got recommend for one medal and they didn't give to me, and I thought that's the one I should have had. Did you ever see the movie -- it's an old movie-- called The Bridges of Tokyo.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: No, I never have.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Well, it's still on TV occasionally. This was with Mickey Rooney and old time movie actor, and Grace Kelly and all of that. Anyway, this was about The Bridges of Tokyo. And actually that was a pretty accurate movie with exception and it wasn't done at the daytime we blew up some bridges at night. So that, that's all.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: That was fun?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: That was kind of fun, and I even wrote it in my book. I've got a book of tales of daring do, and so I put it in there and it was kind of fun. Came back, we knocked these bridges down -- we were volunteering because they had killed a bunch of pilots trying to knock it down in the daytime so we did it at night. I didn't get a medal for that, and I'm still complaining about it.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Well you should, you should have got that medal?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yeah, I should have.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So tell me about your family. How did you stay in touch with them?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Very easy. In World War II, they would write letters, it would be maybe 2 or 3 months before we would get a letter because of the great distances. And they were usually e-mail, which was very tiny little things that were photographed and mailed out all over the world. And we would sometimes write back and it would take so long they didn't know whether you were dead or not for months at a time. And in the Korean war we just had regular letters. In both cases they were free. We could just write -- a lot of people don't know this, we could just write free on the envelope and that was the same as the stamp. And so that's the way we kept in touch both times. I never did talk to my family at all in World War II except when I'd be back in the states for leave or something, and also in the Korean war, we never did use telephones or radios.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: They were even expensive back then?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Even that.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Well, I hesitate to even mention this but it was better than what I had at home in the Navy. It was wonderful. See, now we weren't on the islands. We were in the ships and we had the absolute best food there was. Steaks, pies, and ice cream and the thing we missed in World War II were the fresh vegetables and fruit. And I recall -- and milk. When I came back at the end of World War II, when the aircraft carrier docked and we were released off of the aircraft carrier we were in San Diego, and I recall that the Red Cross had big booths and they were serving milk and the place was jammed with people getting off the ship drinking as much milking as we could.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So they didn't serve milk?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: They had powdered milk and powdered eggs.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: How do you drink powered milk?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: It's powder, just like you can buy at the grocery store now. It's dried milk and you mix water with it. And it wasn't particularly tasteful, and we had plenty of steak and things that would be preserved and stuff. We had canned vegetables and stuff but it was the fresh vegetables and lettuce, we were craving that when we got back and of course -- oh one thing that might be interesting to show you the differences in the services. One of the fleet actions that we were involved in, we had in this great big fleet we had numerous aircraft carriers and around them were, were battleships and heavy cruisers and so on around that, so we were the so called the queen of the fleet. And they always had a ready -- what they called a ready carrier, which meant it was always ready to take airplanes aboard even on a nonscheduled time like someone had an emergency and coming back or else they were going to be dropped in the water. And this one fellow was a British sea fire. He came in landed aboard our ship because he had some damage to his airplane so we in effect rescued him. Of course we had to wait to the time so they could take him back to his aircraft carrier that was operating with us. And so we had dinner that night and we had a normal dinner, we had steaks and food, all kind of good foods and canned goods and pies and ice -- he had pie that I recall that night, and he asked what the celebration was and we said nothing. And so he was amazed that we ate like we did in the American Navy. He said that the British Navy was nothing like that. After we got air superiority in the pacific the Navy had tremendous production, we had all kind of ships and stuff like that and we were just steamed rolled across it.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So being on the ship, how did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Well that wasn't as much fun, we played a lot of _____, a lot of illegal card games and dice games, and I never did do that of course, and which were illegal. We would drink a lot of whiskey that was smuggled in, your not supposed to have any so a lot of times you'd have it smuggled in. But we'd have movies that would be transferred in by a ship that come along a supply ship and send movies or something over like that and we'd see these movies for maybe two weeks at a time. That was fairly sparse. We did a lot of hobbies, a lot of people did reading you know. Some people did school work. I enrolled in Kansas University and I had all my textbooks and I was going to get my college work done while I was there and I never cracked a book. I did one -- start to do one paper and I learned a few days -- I found it on the floor a few days later, we had a party, so I just gave up.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Did you ever go back to finish school?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yes and no. Um, I, and I have to hesitate. I think maybe some of this things that occurred -- I went back to school when I was in my 80's. I got a scholarship believe it or not to Harvard as a special student. But I had gone to -- I'd gone to Kansas University, I'd gone to William Jewell College in Liberty, Missouri, I'd gone to Perdue University, I'd gone to Washburn University in Topeka, Kansas, and I'd gone to another one in Kansas City, Missouri um -- Rockhurst. And I think maybe that some of the things that happened maybe made me, made me do that, or not do that. And after while -- but I did carry pretty much -- I even carried a 3.75 average in Harvard, so I figured well screw you guys I'm as good as you are so anyway, but I never did finish. I have a CLU or a charter lift under designation in the insurance business but I've never gotten a sheep scan, and nowadays I guess I don't even care that much, but i do it to see if I could do it. So the answer is yes I went to a bunch of different colleges. I even went to the art institute and Harvard accepted all my credits, I think I've got a 160 -- a 162 credits but I never did stay in the college long enough to justify the sheep skin.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: It's never to late Mr. Brown.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: We'll I've heard that. And I went as far as getting enrolled in UTA over here and then I got diverted to something else. So I think maybe this, I think maybe the -- what do they call them, the PSP has affected me more than I had thought at the time.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Okay. Well, do you recall any particular unusual event?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Oh yeah, lost of those. Like the time I got court marshalled was one. But there was a lot of funny ones that had happened. One time in World War II, when I was based with those Marines, we lived in some quonset huts. We'd gone from tents, we slept under the -- we slept at one time under the wings of the airplanes, we would have sandbags around them and you know so they wouldn't get hit, we had -- we had quonset huts those big metal buildings that were made that they had latter part of the war. And so one night we had this particular was head quarters quonset hut, and so we had our operations or our ready room they called it up in the top of it, and because of sheer space. And one night it was very dark, and you couldn't even see your hand in front of your face, if your ever in the tropics -- if you ever get a chance to go to the tropics or something you'll observe that it's absolutely black and you can't see, and on a dark night -- anyway, my commanding officer, unknown to me, stepped in front of us four of us were walking upstairs on the outside and so the guy that was in front of me stepped off for some reason and went the other way and then the commanding officer walked up in front of me and so on the way up I goosed him like this and he said, " ____ Brown, what do you think your doing?" And I said "oh I'm sorry sir I thought your were my friend", and he said "I'm not that good of friend!" (Laughter) And so there's a few dumb things like that. Another time, other then being stupid, more stupid -- under stress, some of us had severe stress at times, and -- um one of my seniors -- we had some really, really bad times and we were coming in at night and it had been building up over a period of months of terrible things. And so, he -- we couldn't -- we couldn't make it, we knew we would run out of fuel and so we finally found the aircraft carrier after all kinds of trouble, and so coming in you couldn't even hardly see it at all. We could only see the wake of it, and so I knew I couldn't make it I sure I was going to crash in the sea and so was he, and so he made he -- I'm using my hands again, please forgive me -- but he made his turn and I -- instead of braking -- we called it braking, one airplane brakes from the other one -- and so I didn't brake, I just tucked in real tight and had all my lights off and left them off. And he came around to make his approach and I knew he was too fast and so he got a wave, what they call a wave off, and when -- in those days they had people that did the controlling and so they waved him off like this, they had a -- what they had a black light and so that ment that you had to not land no matter what, even if you killed yourself and so he got this wave off and the guy giving the controls recognized that there was something behind him, and so he recognized and must have been known what it was and he saw me with no lights and is he gave me a -- a cut and so I landed on the carrier and went floating down the -- down the thing, and of course those were called straight deck carriers in those days so we had gone out -- when daylight came that was all stacked up herewith the bombs and stuffed on them. And so they had these big barriers, 3 of them, and they raised them and so I caught the last, I caught the last wire and they dropped the first two and I was so close to it that my propeller skimmed the yellow paint off the tip of it and so they dropped it forward. By this time, and I was out of fuel, this time my fellow that had taken a waive off came behind me and he was still fast, and he hit -- he didn't catch a wire at all, he hit the first barrier and tore it out of the roots and hit the second barrier and tore it out of the roots and the third one it broke and the wires of the barrier wrapped around his cannons and of course in those -- the cannons carried the shell and the chamber and this thing fired when he was in midair and went whizzing past my head and exploded in a plane in front of me just as I was getting out of my plane then he went into the ground and into the deck nose down and caught on fire and of course when he did all of the flood lights came on, and so they said that I jumped out, of course I cared a side arm, I jumped up in my seat and I was going the SOB like this, I had a gun on him and of course there was the admiral and the staff up watching this thing and I had a big, a big plane captain grabbing me and through me down. So they guarded me and they rescued him. He was only burned a little bit so I was grounded for a short time and the next night he's -- this fellow who had just survived the crash the night before that I tried to shoot. He kept talking around the ship that he was not going to be high and fast tonight and so he took my plane and I warned him, my plane had never been hit. Oh I had two holes in it, but it had my name in gold and I was very proud of that. So he took my plane and that night he came back and crashed again and broke my plane in half and the tail fell into the fantail and he slipped burning at the deck again and I was up there watching this and I was on the same level as the staff and the admiral and I must have yelled because I said, "well you SOB I should have shot you last night" and so then they grabbed the both of us, and so we were grounded for about three or four days and then the ship went back for replenishing and it was Christmas time. And so they said that everybody could go and have fun except us and we had to go fly out at some Army base and so we were supposed to practice our flying out there, kind of as a disciplinary action. And they didn't realize that we were, that we were pretty close to loosing our mind, and so we did, we flew across -- we flew from the ship over to the Army base and practiced a couple of landings and then found some mysterious things wrong with our airplanes and said their unsafe to fly and so we went back, and of course we carried our uniforms with us in those days, and so we hitchhiked a ride out of base and went and found a party going on and spent there for about a week and never had a cross word every sense.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Never?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Never. We were ordered not to to.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: So you couldn't?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: No we couldn't of. I don't know anybody who kept a diary. And we were ordered not to from the very first at least the fighters and certainly the once in my group.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: If you could would you have?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: No. No, I wouldn't. I have -- what I did do is I stole pictures and I stole some reports the printed reports that we had, particularly in the Korean. I -- I wouldn't say stole them, I got copies of some of the action reports and kept them, some of them I mailed to my dad and mother. And then I recovered most of those and I put those in my book of information I started writing back in the 60's, and so no, I never kept a diary at all.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: But you had a box with memories?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I didn't have them with me. I always stole them and mailed them away.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yes I do. [Interviewed interrupted by door opening] Do they need the space here?

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: No, your okay.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Okay. Yeah, my service ended three different times. World War II, then when I got out I was very bitter about the United States government at the time. And at the end of World War II I was married by that time and living in married officers quarters. And I had a -- those days were -- you could serve under a written contract from year to year, and I had served under one for one year and by this time it was 1946 and I signed another contract for another year and I was going to transition into civilian life. Maybe go to college or whatever, and suddenly they had a big cut back and ten days before Christmas the Navy charged 27,000 of us just like that with no warning what so ever and they said tomorrow you're out of here. And so at that time for the first time I learned that you can't -- and I don't care if you quote me or not, the written contract means nothing. At this time if it had happened now as I was older I would have sued the United States Government. As it was in those days you just, you never ever questioned authority, but today, they just cut us off with no warning whatsoever and no hope. And so I was stranded with no place to go, no job, very little money, and no income, and I to come back and scrounge for the very first to survive.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And where were you when this happened?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I was in Pensacola, Florida. And my -- I didn't have a home you see. My wife was from the little town of Celina, Kansas. I'd never been to Celina, Kansas in my life. And so my mother and father were in a -- working in Kansas City, or my father -- well yeah, but they rented a house. They didn't have any money and no place to go there, and so if you really have to you can survive. And I didn't get a job. In fact the first job I tried to get the guy said, were you an officer? And I said yeah and he said, well I wasn't. He said I don't like officers and he said I don't like your attitude and I said well, okay bye. And so this is what I -- well I had to start. And so I finally went to an insurance company and said I want a job and they said we don't want you, and we don't have any -- and I said I understand you sell insurance on commission and they said yeah but we can't finance you and so I said well, give me a job. And so they did and so I tried knocking on doors and so I knocked on door in the middle of the winter in a place I had never heard of before and luckily survived. Didn't do well, but I survived.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: And that's all that matters.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: That's all that matters, yeah I guess that's why I'm so obnoxious to this day.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Did your military influence your thinking about war of military in general?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I enjoyed. I like the, I like the comradery and I was lucky though. Now, a lot of people are not they've been in terrible times. I was lucky that I survived, I wasn't hurt, I did well, and I enjoyed it. But I quickly learned that it's not a career for you, if you want to go to higher rank because you need to have the professionalism of the academy's and so forth. But I enjoyed it though, I enjoyed what I was doing because I could fly for free and they paid me to fly. And I've gone from open cockpit flight planes, canvas covered to every fighter that they had up until super sonic. And I was flying super sonic when I finally retired.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: How did your service and experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: I think positively. There's some bad spots, but over all positively. One of the things that they -- a lot of people today don't really realize how valuable you really are and what you can do if you want to. But it taught me among others that I would not settle for a routine job. And I would not -- knocking on doors trying to sell life insurance in the middle of winter. But because of the military I knew there were better things and better times coming and sure enough I was lucky, I kept my health thank goodness, and wound up before I retired that I was a person, not of a big company, but a company that operated national in the insurance business. And so that's why I say it affected me positively. I didn't want to settle and dont to this day settle for second best. I might get second best and maybe deserve it, but don't settle for it. But very positive.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Okay Mr. Brown. Is there anything you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: No, I think I've told you all my war stories I believe and I can think of nothing that-- that -- but I thank you for your time and your trouble.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: Thank you Mr. Brown for giving me the chance to interview you. I had a great time interviewing you and learning about your experiences and your memories. And whether you were joking or not in the beginning you are our hero and you still here.

sp.speaker: James LeRoy Brown
sp.p: Thank you, very much.

sp.speaker: Isabel Granados
sp.p: You're welcome. Mr. Brown: Bye.
